title: Alabama Association of Realtors v. Department of Health and Human Services (2021)
summary: Section 361(a) of the Public Health Service Act did not authorize the CDC's nationwide eviction moratorium, because an agency claiming power of vast economic and political significance must point to clear congressional authorization.
notes:
Key line: The per curiam opinion: "It strains credulity to believe that this statute grants the CDC the sweeping authority that it asserts."

Citation: 594 U.S. 758 (2021).

sections.Parties: The applicants were the Alabama Association of Realtors, the Georgia Association of Realtors and several rental property managers who had sued to stop the eviction moratorium. The respondents were the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose Director had issued the moratorium under a delegation of the Surgeon General's authority in 42 C.F.R. 70.2. The Government defended the order as a measure necessary to prevent the interstate spread of COVID-19. The applicants had already won a judgment in the District Court declaring the order unlawful and came to the Supreme Court asking that the stay of that judgment be lifted so that they could enforce it.
sections.Material Facts: In March 2020 the CARES Act imposed a 120 day eviction moratorium on federally assisted or federally financed properties. When it lapsed in July 2020 Congress did not renew it, and in September 2020 the CDC issued its own moratorium covering all residential properties nationwide and backed by criminal penalties. Congress extended that order for one month in December 2020; the CDC then extended it three more times on its own through July 2021. When it expired on July 31 the CDC reimposed it three days later, limited to counties with substantial or high transmission, which then covered most of the country. The CDC relied on section 361(a) of the Public Health Service Act of 1944, which authorizes regulations necessary to prevent the interstate spread of communicable disease and lists inspection, fumigation, disinfection, sanitation, pest extermination and destruction of contaminated animals and articles as examples.
sections.Procedural History: The District Court for the District of Columbia granted summary judgment to the plaintiffs on May 5, 2021, holding that the CDC lacked statutory authority, but stayed its judgment pending appeal. The D.C. Circuit declined to lift the stay, and on June 29, 2021 the Supreme Court also declined, with Justice Kavanaugh concurring on the ground that the moratorium was unlawful but would expire in weeks, and four Justices voting to vacate. After the CDC reimposed the moratorium in August, the plaintiffs returned to the District Court, which said the equities now favored them but that law of the case bound it; the D.C. Circuit again refused relief. The plaintiffs then applied a second time to the Supreme Court, which granted the application and vacated the stay on August 26, 2021.
sections.Issue: The question before the Court was whether the District Court's stay of its own judgment remained justified under the four factor test of Nken v. Holder, which turns first on the likelihood that the party seeking relief will succeed on the merits. That in turn required the Court to decide whether section 361(a) of the Public Health Service Act, read as a whole, gave the CDC authority to impose a nationwide residential eviction moratorium, and whether the sheer scope of the claimed power should affect how the statutory text is read. The Court also had to weigh the harm to landlords against the public interest in slowing the Delta variant.
sections.Holding: The Court vacated the stay, making the District Court's judgment enforceable. It held that the applicants were virtually certain to succeed on the merits because the CDC had exceeded its authority. The second sentence of section 361(a) informs the first by illustrating the kinds of measures Congress had in mind, all of which directly target disease itself, while an eviction moratorium relates to interstate spread only indirectly. Even if the text were ambiguous, Congress must speak clearly before an agency may exercise powers of vast economic and political significance, and section 361(a) was a wafer thin reed for such power. The equities also favored the landlords. If a federal eviction moratorium is to continue, Congress must specifically authorize it.
sections.Reasoning: The per curiam opinion began with the text. The first sentence of section 361(a) speaks broadly of regulations necessary to prevent interstate spread of disease, but the second lists inspection, fumigation, disinfection, sanitation, pest extermination and destruction of infected articles. Those measures target disease directly; the moratorium works only through a chain of assumptions about infected tenants moving between states. Read together, the sentences made it a stretch to find authority for the moratorium. The Court then invoked Utility Air Regulatory Group v. EPA and Brown & Williamson for the principle that Congress must speak clearly when it authorizes powers of vast economic and political significance. The moratorium covered at least eighty percent of the country and six to seventeen million tenants, Congress had appropriated nearly fifty billion dollars in rental assistance as a rough measure of its economic effect, and it intruded on landlord tenant law, a domain of the states. The Government could identify no limit other than the CDC's own judgment of necessity, which would allow orders for free grocery delivery or free internet service. On the equities, landlords faced irreparable loss of rent and of the right to exclude, while the Government had had three more months to distribute assistance and Congress had failed to act despite notice. Citing Youngstown, the Court said agencies may not act unlawfully even in pursuit of desirable ends.

topics.lrs-i-major-questions: The case supplies a significant assertion of power used in the West Virginia line of precedents.
topics.lrs-i-major-questions-rationales: The majority and dissent in West Virginia give different interpretive explanations for this precedent.
topics.lrs-k-ejusdem: The per curiam confined § 361(a) by reading its general 'other measures' language in light of the specific listed measures (inspection, fumigation, disinfection, sanitation, pest extermination).

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Breyer, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, dissented. He argued that the Court should vacate a lower court stay only when that court clearly and demonstrably erred, and that it had not. The modified order was more tailored than the original, applying only in counties with substantial or high transmission and only to tenants who attested to financial need and to having sought assistance. The first sentence of section 361(a) plainly authorized measures the agency judged necessary, and public health agencies had used eviction restrictions to contain disease when the statute was enacted in 1944. The balance of equities also favored leaving the stay in place given the Delta surge, the rising number of cases, and the public interest in preventing the spread of disease. He would have let the case proceed on the ordinary appellate track rather than resolve it on the emergency docket.
learning.why: The course reads it as the clearest early statement of the clear statement approach that West Virginia v. EPA named the major questions doctrine, and as a case that shows how the breadth of a claimed power feeds back into the reading of statutory text.
